abstract.p: Substantial oxidative stress during myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury precipitates cell death and heart failure, for which translatable redox therapies remain scarce. Here, we show that nicotinamide riboside kinase 2 (NMRK2) is rapidly upregulated after reperfusion and exerts redox protection by a previously unrecognized mechanism. We established myocardial I/R injury in mice and hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) injury in cardiomyocytes. By elevating NADPH, restoring NAD+/NADH, increasing GSH/GSSG and activating Trx1, NMRK2 overexpression enhanced cellular antioxidant capacity and reduced oxidative damage during both myocardial I/R and cellular H/R injury. Knockdown of NAD kinase (NADK) abolished these protective effects. Mechanistically, nucleocytoplasmic fractionation and immunofluorescence confirmed robust Yes-associated protein (YAP) nuclear entry in NMRK2-overexpressing cells; Co-IP revealed NMRK2-induced disruption of the integrin β–YAP interaction; knockdown of integrin β reduced NADK expression and increased YAP phosphorylation at Ser127; and ChIP-qPCR and luciferase assays demonstrated that YAP directly binds the NADK promoter (−1500 to −1000 bp) for its transcriptional activation. In conclusion, NMRK2 sustains redox protection by disrupting the integrin β–YAP complex and driving YAP-dependent NADK transcription, providing a readily translatable therapy against myocardial I/R injury.

list-item.p: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis restores NADPH and limits myocardial I/R injury.
NMRK2 boosts GSH and Trx1 antioxidant systems to curb oxidative stress.
YAP binds NADK promoter (−1500/−1000 bp) after integrin β release.
Findings offer a translatable strategy against acute myocardial I/R injury.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury remains the foremost complication of reperfusion therapy for acute myocardial infarction [[1], [2], [3]]. While restoration of coronary blood flow limits infarct size, it simultaneously triggers an oxidative burst that depletes NADPH, overwhelms the glutathione (GSH) and thioredoxin (Trx) antioxidant systems, and precipitates cardiomyocyte death [[4], [5], [6], [7]]. Effective redox-targeted interventions applicable to this acute reperfusion window remain an urgent unmet clinical need.

NADPH regeneration depends on NAD kinase (NADK)-mediated phosphorylation of NAD+ to NADP+ [8]; making NADK an attractive target for restoring redox balance during early reperfusion. Nicotinamide riboside kinase 2 (NMRK2), the rate-limiting enzyme of the NAD+ salvage pathway, is markedly upregulated within 24 h of reperfusion [9,10]. However, whether it governs NADK transcription or merely supports NAD+ synthesis is unknown. Consequently, the signaling cascades that acutely upregulate NADK during myocardial I/R injury remain undefined.

Here, we demonstrate that NMRK2 mobilizes the Yes-associated protein (YAP)–NADK pathway to replenish NADPH during early reperfusion, thereby restoring the GSH and Trx antioxidant systems and attenuating injury following myocardial I/R in mice and hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) in cardiomyocytes. We present a previously unrecognized NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis positions NADK as a signal-responsive redox node and offer a translatable strategy for acute cardioprotection against myocardial I/R injury.

sec.title: Animals
sec.p: Healthy adult male C57BL/6 mice (20–25 g, 8–10 weeks) were obtained from Suzhou Cavins Biological Model Animal Research Co., Ltd (Suzhou, China; license number: SCXK [Jiangsu] 2018-0002). Mice were housed under a 12-h light/dark cycle (22 ± 2 °C, 50–60% humidity) with free access to standard chow and water. All experimental procedures conformed to the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (NIH, USA). The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Soochow University.

sec.title: Adeno-associated virus Serotype 9 (AAV9)-mediated NMRK2 overexpression
sec.p: AAV9-cTnT-NMRK2 vectors containing an independent green fluorescent reporter (GdGreen), as well as control AAV9-cTnT-GdGreen vectors, were constructed and packaged by OBiO Technology (Shanghai, China). The GdGreen reporter was not fused to the NMRK2 protein and was used solely to monitor viral transduction efficiency. Mice received a single tail-vein injection 3 weeks before myocardial I/R surgery. Successful viral transduction was verified through immunofluorescence staining of myocardial tissue sections. NMRK2 overexpression was validated using protein quantification assays.

sec.title: Myocardial I/R model in mice
sec.p: Mice were anesthetized by intraperitoneal injection of 1% pentobarbital sodium (50 mg/kg). Following tracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation was maintained using a rodent ventilator (Shenzhen Ruiwode Life Technology Co., Ltd., China). A left thoracotomy was performed through the fourth intercostal space to expose the heart. The left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD) was ligated approximately 3 mm below the inferior border of the left atrium using a 6-0 silk suture fashioned into a slipknot. Successful myocardial ischemia was confirmed by cyanosis of the left ventricular myocardium and ST-segment elevation on the electrocardiogram (ECG). After 30 min of ischemia, the ligature was released for reperfusion, and the chest was closed. Upon recovery from anesthesia, the mice were returned to their cages and allowed free access to food and water.

sec.title: Evans blue/2,3,5-triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) double staining
sec.p: At the end of reperfusion, the LAD was re-ligated and a 1% Evans blue solution (Cat No. E2129, Sigma) was injected into the inferior vena cava to delineate the perfused myocardium. The hearts were subsequently excised, rinsed with ice-cold saline, frozen at −80 °C for 15 min, and sliced into 2-mm transverse sections. Slices were incubated in a phosphate buffer solution (pH 7.4) containing 1% TTC (Sigma, T8877) in phosphate buffer (pH 7.4, 37 °C, 30 min), fixed in 4 % paraformaldehyde (Cat No. BL539A, Biosharp, China), and photographed. Infarct size (IS) and area-at-risk (AAR) were quantified with ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health). The extent of myocardial infarction was evaluated by calculating the ratio of IS to AAR (IS/AAR).

sec.title: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining
sec.p: Paraformaldehyde-fixed (4%) hearts were paraffin-embedded and cut into 5-μm transverse sections. After deparaffinization and graded ethanol rehydration, sections were stained with hematoxylin for 5 min and counterstained with eosin for 30 s. After staining, the sections were mounted with neutral resin and examined under a light microscope.

sec.title: Echocardiography
sec.p: Seven days after myocardial I/R injury, mice were anesthetized with 1–2% isoflurane. Two-dimensional and M-mode images were obtained using a high-resolution small-animal ultrasound system from the parasternal short-axis view at the level of the papillary muscles. Left ventricular ejection fraction (EF), fractional shortening (FS), and left ventricular internal diameters at end-diastole (LVID-d) and end-systole (LVID-s) were measured (averaged over 3 consecutive cycles). Image acquisition and analysis were performed in a blinded manner.

sec.title: Tissue apoptosis assessment
sec.p: Apoptotic cells in myocardial tissues were evaluated using terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL) combined with 4’,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) counterstaining. Paraffin sections (5 μm) were deparaffinized, rehydrated, and digested with 20 μg/mL proteinase K (Roche) for 15 min at room temperature. Endogenous peroxidase activity was quenched with 3% hydrogen peroxide. Subsequently, the sections were incubated with 50 μL of TUNEL reaction mixture (In Situ Cell Death Detection Kit, Roche) at 37 °C for 1 h, counterstained with DAPI. TUNEL-positive apoptotic cells (green fluorescence) and DAPI-stained nuclei (blue fluorescence) were visualized under a fluorescence microscope (Olympus BX50). The apoptotic index was calculated as the ratio of TUNEL-positive cells to the total number of DAPI-positive nuclei.

sec.title: Measurement of ROS
sec.p: Intracellular and tissue ROS levels were assessed using dihydroethidium (DHE) and 2′,7′-dichlorofluorescin diacetate (DCFH-DA) staining. For in vivo detection, unfixed frozen heart sections (10 μm) were incubated with 10 μM DHE (Sigma-Aldrich, D7008) at 37 °C for 30 min in a dark humidified chamber. Ethidium-derived fluorescence was visualized using a fluorescence microscope (Nikon Eclipse Ti-SR) at 200 × magnification with excitation/emission wavelengths set at 488/610 nm. Fluorescence intensity was quantified using Image-Pro Plus software (version 6.0). For in vitro analysis, H9c2 and AC16 cells were seeded in 6-well plates (60% confluence) and incubated with 10 μM DCFH-DA (Beyotime S0033S) diluted in serum-free medium at 37 °C for 20 min. Cells were washed three times and fluorescence signal was captured using a fluorescence microscope (excitation at 488 nm and emission at 522 nm). ROS production was measured by quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity using ImageJ software.

sec.title: Western blotting
sec.p: Hearts harvested 24 h post-reperfusion were frozen, homogenized in ice-cold RIPA buffer (Beyotime P0013B) plus 1 mM PMSF, and centrifuged (14800×g, 30 min, 4 °C). Supernatant extracts were aspirated and protein concentration was determined using the BCA method. Equal amounts of total protein were loaded into each well and separated by 10% sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. Following electrophoresis, the proteins were transferred onto a polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membrane, which was subsequently blocked with 5% non-fat milk in 1 × Tris-buffered saline tween (TBST) buffer for 2 h, followed by overnight incubation with primary antibodies at 4 °C. The details of primary antibodies are available in Supplementary Table 1. After three TBST washes, HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (CoWin, 1:4000) were applied at room temperature for 2 h. Immunoblot bands were visualized using an electrochemiluminescence kit (Tanon, China) and quantified by ImageJ. Data are expressed as the ratios of target/β-tubulin density.

sec.title: Cell culture
sec.p: Human AC16 cardiomyocyte-like cells and rat H9c2 cardiomyoblasts (Zhongqiao Xinzhou Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) were cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM)/F12 medium or DMEM, respectively, each supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco 10099-141C) at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2. Cells were passaged every 2–3 days at a ratio of 1:3 and used for experiments upon reaching 70–80% confluency.

sec.title: NMRK2 overexpression
sec.p: NMRK2 overexpression was achieved by plasmid transfection (for immunofluorescence/flow cytometry) or lentiviral transduction (for protein and biochemical assays). For plasmid delivery, FLAG-tagged NMRK2 vector (GenePharma, Suzhou) was transfected with Transfect-Mate reagent (Cat. No. 220901) according to the manufacturer's instructions; FLAG expression was verified by Western blotting. For lentiviral delivery, GFP-NMRK2 particles (OBiO Technology, Shanghai) were added at a multiplicity of infection of 1 × 108 TU/mL; successful transduction was confirmed by GFP fluorescence and NMRK2 protein levels. Both methods provided efficient and consistent NMRK2 overexpression tailored to specific experimental needs.

sec.title: In vitro hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R)
sec.p: Cells were washed with PBS and incubated in glucose-free DMEM (Procell PM150271), then transferred to a hypoxic workstation (37 °C, 95% N2/5% CO2) for 6 h. After hypoxia, cells were returned to standard conditions (complete DMEM/F12 medium supplemented with 10 % FBS). Reoxygenation was conducted in a standard incubator with 95% air/5% CO2 at 37 °C for 3 h.

sec.title: Cell viability
sec.p: Cell viability was evaluated using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; ApexBio K1018). Cells were seeded in 96-well plates (1 × 104 cells/well) and cultured under standard conditions for 24 h. After the indicated treatments, 10 μL of CCK-8 reagent was added directly to the culture medium in each well, followed by incubation at 37 °C for 1 h. Absorbance at 450 nm was subsequently recorded on a microplate reader. Viability is expressed relative to untreated controls.

sec.title: Live/dead cell staining
sec.p: Cell death was assessed using the LIVE/DEAD Cell Imaging Kit (Thermo Fisher R37601). Live cells were labeled with calcein-AM, which is enzymatically converted into green-fluorescent calcein, whereas dead cells were identified by red fluorescence from ethidium homodimer-1 staining of cells with compromised membranes. Following H/R, AC16 and H9c2 cells were incubated with a 2 × working solution at 22 °C for 15 min. Fluorescent signals were immediately captured using a fluorescence microscope, with live cells appearing green and dead cells appearing red. Three random fields per well were analyzed and experiments were performed in triplicate.

sec.title: Flow cytometry
sec.p: Apoptosis was quantified using Annexin V-FITC/PI double staining (Beyotime C1062 M). After H/R, cells were washed, resuspended in binding buffer, and incubated with Annexin V-FITC followed by PI according to the kit protocol. For ROS detection, cells were incubated with 10 μM DCFH-DA (20 min, 37 °C) or 10 μM DHE (30 min, 37 °C, dark). After staining, cells were washed and analyzed using a CytoFLEX™ flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA). Data were processed and analyzed with FlowJo software.

sec.title: NAD+/NADH, NADP+/NADPH, and GSH/GSSG measurements
sec.p: NAD+ and NADH levels were measured using the WST-8 NAD+/NADH Assay Kit (Beyotime S0175). NADP+ and NADPH levels were measured using the WST-8 NADP+/NADPH Assay Kit (Beyotime S0179). GSH and GSSG levels were quantified utilizing the GSH and GSSG Assay Kit (Beyotime S0053).

sec.title: Lipid peroxidation assay
sec.p: Lipid peroxidation was assessed using the malondialdehyde (MDA) Assay Kit (Beyotime S0131S). Briefly, samples were processed, and reaction products were quantified using a microplate reader. MDA concentrations were determined by referencing the standard curve provided in the kit instructions.

sec.title: Nuclear and cytoplasmic protein extraction
sec.p: Nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins were isolated from cardiomyocytes using the Cytoplasmic and Nuclear Protein Extraction Kit (Beyotime P0027). Briefly, cells were lysed with Buffer A (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0; 10 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, and 0.5% (v/v) NP-40) and incubated for 20 min. The cytoplasmic fraction was collected by centrifugation at 12,000×g for 5 min. The nuclear pellets were washed with Buffer A and resuspended in Buffer B (20 mM Hepes, pH 7.9; 0.5 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, and 1 mM dithiothreitol). After a 20-min incubation, the nuclear fraction was collected by centrifugation at 12,000×g for 10 min.

sec.title: RNA extraction and Real-time quantitative PCR
sec.p: Total RNA was extracted from heart tissue using Trizol reagent (Thermo Fisher 15596026). RNA quality and purity were evaluated using UV spectrophotometry (NanoDrop 2000; Thermo Fisher) by measuring absorbance at 260 and 280 nm, respectively. For cDNA synthesis, 1 μg total RNA was used as the template. The qPCR reaction mixture contained 5 μL SYBR qPCR SuperMix (Novoprotein E096-01A), 1 μL forward and reverse primers, 1 μL cDNA, and 2 μL RNase-free water. Cycling conditions included 40 amplifications followed by melting curve analysis. Target gene (NMRK2, NADK) expression was normalized to β-tubulin using the 2−ΔΔCt method; primers were synthesized by Qingke Biotechnology (Beijing).

sec.title: NMRK2, NADK and integrin β knockdown with siRNA
sec.p: All small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) were synthesized by GenePharma Co., Ltd. (Suzhou, China). Cells were seeded into 6-well plates, cultured in antibiotic-free medium for 24 h, washed with PBS, and transfected with 25 nM siRNA using GP-transfect-Mate reagent. Cells were subsequently incubated at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2 for 48 h for gene expression analysis or 72 h for protein analysis and functional assays. All integrin β antibodies and siRNAs used in this study specifically targeted integrin β1.

sec.title: Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP)
sec.p: Protein–protein interactions between Integrin β and YAP were examined by Co-IP assays. Cardiomyocytes were lysed in ice-cold IP lysis buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. After centrifugation at 12,000×g for 15 min at 4 °C, equal amounts of total protein were incubated overnight at 4 °C with anti-integrin β1 antibody or control IgG, followed by incubation with protein A/G agarose beads for 2 h. The beads were then washed extensively with lysis buffer, and bound proteins were eluted by boiling in SDS sample buffer. Immunoprecipitated proteins and input lysates were analyzed by western blotting using antibodies against YAP and Integrin β.

sec.title: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-qPCR
sec.p: ChIP assays were performed using a commercial ChIP kit (CST 9005S) to assess the binding of YAP to the NADK promoter. Cardiomyocytes were cross-linked with 1% formaldehyde at room temperature for 10 min and quenched with glycine. Cells were then lysed, and chromatin was sheared by sonication to obtain DNA fragments of approximately 200–500 bp. The fragmented chromatin was incubated overnight at 4 °C with an anti-YAP antibody or normal IgG as a negative control. Immunocomplexes were captured using protein A/G magnetic beads, washed extensively, and eluted. Cross-links were reversed, and DNA was purified and analyzed by qPCR using primers targeting the NADK promoter. Results were normalized to input DNA and presented as fold enrichment over IgG controls.

sec.title: Luciferase reporter assay
sec.p: To evaluate YAP-dependent transcriptional activation of the NADK promoter, truncated NADK promoter fragments (−2000/0, −1500/0, −1000/0, and −500/0 relative to the transcription start site) were cloned into a firefly luciferase reporter vector. Cardiomyocytes were co-transfected with these constructs and a YAP expression plasmid or control vector, along with a Renilla luciferase plasmid as an internal control. Luciferase activity was measured 24–48 h later using a dual-luciferase assay system. Firefly luciferase activity was normalized to Renilla luciferase activity and expressed as relative luciferase activity.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Data from the GSE160516 dataset were processed using R software and various online bioinformatic tools. Experimental data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 8 software. Continuous variables are expressed as mean ± standard error of mean (SEM). For the comparison between two groups, a two-sided unpaired Student's t-test was conducted, while differences among multiple groups were examined using either one-way or two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's multiple comparisons test. A P value < 0.05 was deemed statistically significant.

sec.title: NMRK2 is markedly upregulated during early phase of myocardial I/R injury
sec.p:
Transcriptomic analysis of the GSE160516 dataset identified NMRK2 among the most prominently upregulated genes at 24 h after myocardial I/R injury (Fig. 1A–C). Consistently, in our mouse myocardial I/R model, coronary occlusion produced obvious ST-segment elevation and significant arrythmias was noted during reperfusion (Fig. 1D). Western blotting corroborated the transcriptomic signature, revealing a marked increase in NMRK2 protein expression at 24 h of reperfusion, coinciding with elevated apoptotic markers (cleaved-PARP and cleaved-caspase 3) (Fig. 1E–H).Fig. 1
Identification of Nmrk2 as a key gene in mouse myocardial I/R injury. (A) Volcano plot of GSE160516 showing DEGs between I/R 24 h and sham mouse heart samples (orange dots, significantly upregulated genes; blue dots, significantly downregulated genes; adjusted p-value <0.05 and |log2FC| ≥ 1). (B) Heatmap of the top 20 DEGs. Each column represents an individual sample, while each row indicates a specific gene. The color scale reflects relative gene expression level (blue, lower expression; orange, higher expression) (n = 4). (C) Transcriptional expression of Nmrk2 in sham samples and samples subjected to I/R 6, 24, and 48 h in GSE160516 (n = 4). (D) Representative electrocardiographic patterns under normal conditions, during ischemia, and during reperfusion in mouse myocardial I/R model. (E) Representative immunoblot bands showing time-dependent expression of NMRK2, cleaved-PARP, and cleaved-caspase 3 in myocardial tissues. (F–H) Analysis of NMRK2, cleaved-PARP and cleaved-caspase 3 proteins in sham and I/R groups at 3, 6, and 24 h of reperfusion (n = 5). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. One-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test for comparisons. **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001. DEGs, differentially expressed genes; FC, fold change; I/R, ischemia/reperfusion.Fig. 1

sec.title: NMRK2 attenuates myocardial I/R injury by inhibiting apoptosis and oxidative stress
sec.p:
Successful transfection was observed 3 weeks after tail-vein delivery of AAV9-cTnT-NMRK2 (Fig. 2A, Supplement Fig. 1). Western blotting showed significantly increased NMRK2 protein expression in mouse cardiac tissue (Fig. 2B and C). Evans blue/TTC double staining demonstrated a pronounced reduction in infarct size relative to area-at-risk in NMRK2-overexpressing hearts following I/R injury (Fig. 2D–F), and H&E sections exhibited less histopathological damage of myocardium (Fig. 2G and H). Echocardiographic assessment further revealed that NMRK2 overexpression mitigated the decline in left-ventricular EF and FS, while limiting LVID-s and LVID-d, 7 days after reperfusion (Fig. 2I–M).Fig. 2
NMRK2 protects against myocardial I/R injury in mice. (A) Schematic of NMRK2 overexpression by tail vein injection of AAV-cTNT-GdGreen-NMRK2 or control AAV-cTNT-GdGreen-Vector. After 3 weeks, mice were subjected to 30-min myocardial ischemia followed by 24-h reperfusion. (B–C) Representative immunoblot bands and analysis of NMRK2 protein expression in myocardial tissues (n = 5). (D) Representative images of Evans blue/TTC staining of myocardium in sham and I/R mice with or without NMRK2 overexpression. (E–F) Quantitative analysis of myocardial infarct size (n = 5). (G–H) Representative H&E staining and quantitative analysis of myocardial structural damage. Scale bar: 50 μm (n = 5). (I–M) Representative M-mode echocardiographic images and quantitative analysis of left ventricular EF, FS, LVID-s and LVID-d (n = 3). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Unpaired Student's t-test or one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for comparisons. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001. AAV, adeno-associated virus; GdGreen, green fluorescent reporter; I/R, ischemia/reperfusion; NC, negative control; TTC, triphenyltetrazolium chloride; AAR, area at risk; LV, left ventricle; IA, infarct area; H&E, hematoxylin and eosin; EF, ejection fraction; FS, fractional shortening; LVID-s, left ventricular internal diameter at systole; LVID-d, left ventricular internal diameter at diastole.Fig. 2

This functional protection was accompanied by a marked decrease in myocardial apoptosis and oxidative burden. TUNEL staining showed fewer positively labeled nuclei in NMRK2-overexpressing mice (Fig. 3A and B), and DHE and DCFH-DA fluorescence staining indicated a parallel attenuation of ROS generation (Fig. 3C and D). Consistently, Western blotting (Fig. 4A) showed that NMRK2 overexpression significantly increased the protein expression of NMRK2 and NADK (Fig. 4B and C), downregulated cleaved-PARP and cleaved-caspase 3 (Fig. 4D and E), upregulated the antioxidant enzymes SOD1 and SOD2 (Fig. 4F and G), and enhanced the expression of the thioredoxin-1 system components Trx1 and Prdx1 (Fig. 4H and I).Fig. 3
NMRK2 reduces myocardial I/R-induced apoptosis and ROS generation in mice. (A–B) Representative immunofluorescence images and analysis of TUNEL-positive cells. Scale bar: 50 μm (n = 5). (C–D) Representative immunofluorescence images and analysis of ROS-positive cells. Scale bar: 50 μm (n = 5). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for comparisons. ***P < 0.001. I/R, ischemia/reperfusion; NC, negative control; DAPI, 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole; TUNEL, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling; ROS, reactive oxygen species.Fig. 3Fig. 4
NMRK2 modulates apoptosis- and oxidative stress-related proteins in myocardial I/R injury. (A) Representative immunoblot bands showing the expression of key proteins related to apoptosis and oxidative stress in myocardial tissues from sham and I/R mice with or without NMRK2 overexpression. (B–G) Analysis of protein expression of NMRK2, NADK, cleaved-PARP, cleaved-caspase 3, SOD1, SOD2, Trx1, and Prdx1 (n = 5). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for comparisons. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001. I/R, ischemia/reperfusion; NC, negative control.Fig. 4

sec.title: NMRK2 protects cardiomyocytes against H/R injury by suppressing apoptosis and oxidative stress
sec.p:
In H9c2 and AC16 cardiomyocytes subjected to H/R injury, Western blotting showed that NMRK2 protein expression rose progressively during reoxygenation (Fig. 5A–D). Hypoxia for 6 h followed by 3-h reoxygenation (H6R3) resulted in the most severe cell injury (Fig. 5E and F). NMRK2 overexpression was performed via lentiviral or plasmid-mediated transfection (Fig. 5G), which was validated by the increased expression of Flag-NMRK2 in both H9c2 (Fig. 5H and I) and AC16 cells (Fig. 5J and K). NMRK2 overexpression significantly improved cell viability following H/R injury (Fig. 5L and M). Additionally, H/R treatment led to extensive cardiomyocyte death, whereas NMRK2 overexpression significantly increased the proportion of living cells in both H9c2 (Fig. 6A and B) and AC16 cardiomyocytes (Fig. 6C and D).Fig. 5
NMRK2 protects against H/R injury in H9c2 and AC16 cardiomyocytes. (A–D) Representative immunoblots showing H/R-induced time-dependent changes in NMRK2 protein expression in H9c2 and AC16 cardiomyocytes (n = 5). (E–F) CCK-8 assay showing cell viability during reoxygenation in both cardiomyocytes (n = 6). (G) Schematic of NMRK2 overexpression in cardiomyocytes via lentiviral or plasmid-mediated transfection. (H–K) Representative immunoblots and analysis of NMRK2 protein expression in H9c2 and AC16 cardiomyocytes (n = 5). (L–M) CCK-8 assay showing that NMRK2 overexpression significantly improved cell viability in both cardiomyocytes (n = 6). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Unpaired Student's t-test or one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for comparisons. *P < 0.05, ***P < 0.001. H/R, hypoxia/reoxygenation; NC, negative control; LV, lentivirus; PL, plasmid; CCK-8, Cell Counting Kit-8.Fig. 5Fig. 6
NMRK2 reduces cell death following H/R injury in H9c2 and AC16 cardiomyocytes. (A–B) Representative live/dead cell staining images and analysis of living cell ratio in H9c2 cardiomyocytes. Scale bar: 50 μm (n = 5). (C–D) Representative live/dead cell staining images and analysis of living cell ratio in AC16 cardiomyocytes. Scale bar: 50 μm (n = 5). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for comparisons. ***P < 0.001. H/R, hypoxia/reoxygenation; NC, negative control.Fig. 6

Western blotting showed that NMRK2 overexpression decreased the H/R-induced expression of cleaved-PARP and cleaved-caspase 3 in both cell lines (Fig. 7A–F), and flow cytometry of Annexin V-FITC/PI staining confirmed a significant drop in the apoptotic populations (Fig. 7G–J). Parallel measurements of oxidative stress showed that NMRK2 overexpression attenuated the H/R-induced surge of ROS (Fig. 8A–H). Western blotting indicated that NMRK2 overexpression exerted antioxidant effects, as reflected by the upregulated expression of SOD1 and SOD2 (Fig. 8I–N). Additionally, the level of MDA (an indicator of lipid peroxidation) was significantly elevated after H/R injury and was reduced by NMRK2 overexpression (Fig. 8O and P). We further assessed the endogenous role of NMRK2 using siRNA in H9c2 and AC16 cardiomyocytes. NMRK2 knockdown significantly aggravated H/R-induced cell injury, as evidenced by reduced cell viability (assessed at H6R24), increased ROS production, and elevated expression of apoptotic markers cleaved-PARP and cleaved-caspase 3 (Supplementary Fig. 2–3).Fig. 7

One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for comparisons. **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001. sec.title: NMRK2 sustains redox homeostasis during H/R injury via transcriptionally activating NADK
sec.p:
Given that NMRK2 salvages NAD+ and NADPH is the principal reductant for antioxidant systems [11], we first assessed NAD(H) and NADP(H) balance and downstream redox markers. NMRK2 overexpression reversed the H/R-induced decline in NAD+, NAD+ + NADH, the NAD+/NADH ratio, NADPH, and the NADPH/NADP+ ratio without altering NADH (Fig. 9A–H), indicating an improved redox state and enhanced antioxidant capacity.Fig. 9
NMRK2 modulates redox balance and activates NADK and Trx1 system in H/R injury. (A–H) NMRK2 overexpression modulates NAD+, NADH, NADP+ and NADPH levels in AC16 cardiomyocytes under H/R conditions (n = 5). (I–K) Measurement of GSH and GSSG levels, as well as the GSH/GSSG ratio (n = 5). (L–O) Representative immunoblots and analysis of NADK, Trx1, and Prdx1 protein expression following H/R and NMRK2 overexpression (n = 5). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for comparisons. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001. H/R, hypoxia/reoxygenation; NC, negative control; GSH, reduced glutathione; GSSG, oxidized glutathione; NAD+, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide; NADH, reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide; NADP+, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate; NADPH, reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate.Fig. 9

NADPH serves as the electron donor that keeps both the GSH and Trx1 systems in their active states [[12], [13], [14]]. H/R treatment significantly reduced the level of GSH and GSH/GSSG ratio, while NMRK2 overexpression increased GSH, GSSG, and the GSH/GSSG ratio to enhance the antioxidant defense (Fig. 9I–K). Additionally, NADK, Trx1, and Prdx1 were further upregulated by NMRK2 overexpression (Fig. 9L–O). These changes prompted us to test whether NADK operates as a downstream effector of NMRK2-mediated redox regulation. Next, we performed NADK knockdown using four different siRNA oligos, of which siRNA-3 was the most effective one (Fig. 10A and B). NADK knockdown significantly abrogated the NMRK2-mediated increase in NADK, Trx1, Prdx1, SOD1, and SOD2, and concomitantly abolished the anti-apoptotic and survival-promoting effects of NMRK2 (Fig. 10C–I, Supplement Fig. 4), confirming that NADK is required for the antioxidant program.Fig. 10
NMRK2 activates NADK and antioxidant system in H/R injury. (A–B) Representative immunoblots and analysis of NADK knockdown efficiency using four siRNA constructs in AC16 cardiomyocytes (n = 5). (C–I) Representative immunoblots and protein expression analysis of NMRK2, NADK, Trx1, Prdx1, SOD1, and SOD2 under the treatments of NADK knockdown and NMRK2 overexpression during H/R injury (n = 5). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for comparisons. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001. H/R, hypoxia/reoxygenation; NC, negative control; siRNA, small interfering RNA.Fig. 10

sec.title: NMRK2 upregulates NADK during H/R injury via the YAP signaling pathway
sec.p:
Real-time qPCR showed that NMRK2 overexpression raised NADK mRNA expression, suggesting a potential transcriptional regulation (Fig. 11A). Given that NMRK2 is an integrin-binding protein and the YAP signaling pathway plays a crucial role in regulating integrin family proteins [[15], [16], [17]], we next examined how NMRK2 overexpression influences YAP activity and its upstream regulator MST1. Western blotting showed that H/R injury resulted in upregulation of MST1, phosphorylation of MST1 (p-MST1), and phosphorylation of YAP (p-YAP), while YAP was decreased (Fig. 11B–F). In contrast, NMRK2 overexpression significantly reduced p-MST1 and p-YAP.Fig. 11
NMRK2 regulates NADK via YAP signaling pathway in H/R injury. (A) qPCR analysis showing a significant upregulation of NADK mRNA expression in AC16 cardiomyocytes with NMRK2 overexpression (n = 5). (B–F) Representative immunoblots and protein expression analysis of MST1, phosphorylated MST1 (p-MST1), YAP, and phosphorylated YAP (p-YAP) (n = 5). (G–H) Representative immunoblots and analysis of nucleocytoplasmic fractionation of YAP protein (n = 5). (I–J) Representative immunofluorescence imaging and analysis of YAP co-localization with the nuclei in the NMRK2 overexpression group compared to the NC group (n = 5). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Unpaired Student's t-test or one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for comparisons. *P < 0.05, ***P < 0.001. H/R, hypoxia/reoxygenation; NC, negative control; DAPI, 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole.Fig. 11

To further explore the intracellular mechanism, we performed nucleocytoplasmic fractionation and immunofluorescence imaging of YAP expression. Western blotting of separated fractions revealed a significant rise in nuclear YAP and a parallel drop in cytosolic YAP after NMRK2 overexpression under both baseline and H/R conditions, confirming enhanced nuclear translocation (Fig. 11G and H). Immunofluorescence images corroborated this shift, displaying stronger nuclear YAP signal in NMRK2-overexpressing cells than in controls (Fig. 11I and J).

sec.title: Direct integrin β–YAP coupling relays NMRK2 signals to NADK
sec.p:
Co-immunoprecipitation was performed to detect the interaction between integrin β and YAP in cardiomyocytes, showing that YAP resides in integrin β immunocomplexes under basal conditions; Flag-NMRK2 overexpression disrupted this interaction without altering total integrin β or YAP levels (Fig. 12A and B).Fig. 12
NMRK2 modulates the integrin β–YAP interaction to regulate NADK. (A–B) Co-IP analysis showing the interaction between integrin β and YAP in AC16 cardiomyocytes. Cell lysates were immunoprecipitated with anti-integrin β or anti-YAP antibodies (or control IgG), followed by immunoblotting for YAP and integrin β, respectively. MG132 was added to prevent proteasomal degradation. Input samples confirmed comparable expression levels of YAP and integrin β (n = 3). (C) qPCR analysis of NADK mRNA expression following integrin β knockdown using three different siRNAs (n = 5). (D–H) Representative immunoblots and protein expression analysis of NADK, p-YAP, YAP, and integrin β in cardiomyocytes subjected to integrin β knockdown with or without NMRK2 overexpression (n = 5). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for comparisons. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001. Co-IP, co-immunoprecipitation; IgG, immunoglobulin G; IP, immunoprecipitation; IB, immunoblotting; NC, negative control; siRNA, small interfering RNA.Fig. 12

To evaluate the functional contribution of integrin β in YAP-mediated NMRK2-NADK activation, cells were transfected with three independent siRNAs. Real-time qPCR showed that siRNA-1 and siRNA-2 achieved a strong knockdown efficiency (Fig. 12C). Depleting integrin β with either oligo significantly reduced the protein expression of NADK and increased YAP phosphorylation at Ser127. Importantly, integrin β depletion abolished the ability of NMRK2 to elevate NADK and suppress YAP phosphorylation (Fig. 12D–H). Thus, integrin β is indispensable for YAP nuclear shuttling and subsequent activation of NADK.

sec.title: YAP directly regulates NADK transcription
sec.p:
To determine whether YAP directly regulates the transcription of NADK, we performed mechanistic experiments including ChIP-qPCR and luciferase reporter assays (Fig. 13A–C). In ChIP-qPCR with an anti-YAP antibody, YAP immunoprecipitation led to a significant enrichment of the NADK promoter region compared with IgG controls, confirming that YAP occupies the chromatin region in situ (Fig. 13B). To define the responsive element, we generated 5′-truncated luciferase reporters spanning −2000 to −500 bp (Fig. 13A). YAP co-transfection robustly activated the −2000 and −1500 bp fragments, whereas deletion to −1000 bp or −500 bp abolished YAP-induced transcriptional activation (Fig. 13C). These results pinpoint the binding interval between −1500 and −1000 bp upstream of the NADK transcription start site.Fig. 13
YAP directly binds to the NADK promoter and activates its transcription. (A) Schematic illustration of the human NADK promoter region (−2000 to −0 bp relative to the transcription start site) showing putative YAP-binding sites and the design of a series of truncated NADK promoter luciferase reporter constructs. (B) ChIP-qPCR analysis demonstrating significant enrichment of the NADK promoter region in anti-YAP immunoprecipitates compared with IgG controls (n = 3). (C) Luciferase reporter assays showing that YAP overexpression significantly enhances transcriptional activity driven by the −2000/0 and −1500/0 NADK promoter fragments, whereas further truncation to −1000/0 or −500/0 markedly attenuates YAP-induced activation, identifying the YAP-responsive region within the −1500 to −1000 bp interval (n = 3). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Unpaired Student's t-test or one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for comparisons. ***P < 0.001. ChIP, Chromatin immunoprecipitation; IgG, immunoglobulin G; LUC, luciferase; Rluc, Renilla luciferase; NC, negative control.Fig. 13

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Earlier studies have established NMRK2 as a key enzyme in NAD+ salvage pathway and documented its metabolic importance in in heart and skeletal muscle [9,18]. NMRK2 is markedly upregulated in ischemic and hypertensive conditions, and confers protection by suppressing pro-apoptotic/fibrotic gene expression, enhancing mitochondrial function, and maintaining ATP production [19,20]. Conversely, NMRK2 deletion activates p38 MAPK, impairs metabolic adaptation, and exacerbates cardiac dysfunction [21]. These data underscore the critical role of NMRK2 in preserving energy homeostasis and redox balance under stress conditions.

NADPH acts as a critical electron donor for major antioxidant systems and is regenerated via NADK-mediated phosphorylation of NAD+ to NADP+ [[22], [23], [24]]. While NADK is indispensable for redox homeostasis, it has traditionally been viewed as a constitutive housekeeping enzyme with no described transcriptional control in the heart [[25], [26], [27]]. Given that NMRK2 is an integrin-binding protein known to interact with the YAP pathway [15,28], it is plausible that NMRK2 modulates NADK expression through YAP signaling. YAP is increasingly recognized for its critical roles in regulating cellular metabolism, oxidative stress responses, and myocardial regeneration and remodeling. Activation of YAP stimulates cardiomyocyte proliferation and enhances cardioprotective gene expression [29,30]. Additionally, epigenetic modifications of the Hippo-YAP pathway promote YAP translation, support myocardial regeneration, reduce infarct severity, and improve cardiac function [31,32]. However, the signaling cascades related to NMRK2 and NADK during myocardial I/R injury remain unclear.

Here, we performed bioinformatic analysis of the GSE160516 dataset and identified NMRK2 as one of the most prominently upregulated genes within 24 h of reperfusion, a finding corroborated in our murine I/R model. Gain-of-function experiments showed that NMRK2 overexpression reduced infarct size, preserved myocardial architecture, and attenuated oxidative damage during myocardial I/R injury. NMRK2 overexpression also lowered cleaved-caspase 3 and cleaved-PARP while increasing SOD1, SOD2, Trx1 and Prdx1 expression. In cardiomyocytes subjected to H/R, NMRK2 improved cell viability, decreased apoptosis, and curtailed ROS generation. Quantitative metabolite analysis showed that NMRK2 restored NAD+/NADH and NADPH/NADP+ ratios, elevated GSH/GSSG, and enhanced Trx1 activity. These protective effects are completely abolished by NADK knockdown, establishing that NMRK2-mediated antioxidant defense is NADK-dependent.

Previous studies have reported the cardioprotective role of NMRK2 in ischemic cardiac injury and other cardiac diseases [9,10,18,21], but they primarily focused on the metabolic functions of NMRK2. Our work, however, reveals its dual role as both a metabolic and redox regulator. Our data provide the first evidence that NMRK2 rapidly upregulates NADK at the transcriptional level through a YAP-dependent mechanism., providing novel insight into NMRK2-mediated redox protection during myocardial I/R injury. As outlined in Fig. 14, NMRK2 acts as an early sensor of reperfusion stress and disrupts integrin β–YAP tethering at the cytosolic membrane, thereby releasing YAP for nuclear import. Inside the nucleus, YAP binds the NADK promoter (−1500 to −1000 bp) and trans-activates NADK transcription. Concomitantly, NMRK2-driven NAD+ salvage sustains NAD+/NADH balance and supplies substrate for the newly induced NADK. The resulting surge in NADP+/NADPH recharges the GSH and Trx systems, which in turn neutralize ROS and limit oxidative injury. Thus, by linking integrin-mediated mechanical signaling to YAP-dependent transcriptional control of NADPH regeneration, the NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis provides a coherent and translatable strategy for acute cardioprotection against myocardial I/R injury.Fig. 14
Schematic of NMRK2-mediated cardioprotection against myocardial I/R injury. Under myocardial I/R conditions, NMRK2 reduces the integrin β–YAP interaction and facilitates YAP nuclear translocation. After entering the nucleus, YAP directly binds to the NADK promoter region (−1500 to −1000 bp) to promote NADK transcription. In parallel, NMRK2, as a key enzyme in NAD+ metabolism, contributes to maintain intracellular NAD+/NADH homeostasis and provide metabolic support for redox regulation. Upregulation of NADK enhances NADP+/NADPH production, activates the GSH and Trx antioxidant systems, and suppresses ROS accumulation and oxidative stress. Through coordinated regulation of YAP-dependent transcriptional control and NAD(P)H-mediated redox homeostasis, NMRK2 confers robust cardioprotection against myocardial I/R injury. I/R, ischemia/reperfusion; GSH, glutathione; Trx, thioredoxin; ROS, reactive oxygen species; NAD+, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide; NADH, reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide; NADP+, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate; NADPH, reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate.Fig. 14

There are several limitations. First, due to cellular heterogeneity of cardiac tissue and the dynamic regulation of Hippo–YAP signaling in vivo, mechanistic analyses were primarily conducted in cardiomyocyte models; validation of the NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis in primary cardiomyocytes will therefore be important to strengthen translational relevance. In addition, as this study predominantly relies on gain-of-function approaches, future in vivo loss-of-function models will be required to establish the necessity of NMRK2 in myocardial I/R injury. Second, although our data support a model in which NMRK2 modulates YAP activity via integrin-associated signaling, the precise molecular interactions and signaling hierarchy linking NMRK2, integrin complexes, MST1 activity, and YAP regulation remain to be fully defined. Whether MST1 inhibition represents a direct consequence of integrin-dependent signaling or an independent regulatory input into YAP activation warrants further investigation. Moreover, as YAP functions as a transcriptional co-activator, future studies dissecting relevant TEAD isoforms and potential integrin β subtype specificity will further refine the transcriptional control of NADK expression. Finally, beyond redox regulation and apoptosis, the roles of NMRK2 in mitochondrial energetics, inflammation, and long-term cardiac remodeling remain to be explored. Consistent with the temporal scope of the present study, functional analyses were limited to the early post-I/R phase, and effects on chronic remodeling and progression to heart failure will require longer-term investigation.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: We uncover the NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis underlying myocardial I/R injury, in which NMRK2 senses reperfusion stress, disengages YAP from integrin β, and mobilizes YAP-dependent NADK transcription to replenish NADPH and restore antioxidant capacity. These findings offer a readily translatable therapeutic strategy for reducing myocardial I/R injury in high-risk patients.
